item.title: Leiden University and Riverlane Research Reveals Distance-Losing Flaw in Correlated Decoding Below Threshold
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article is important because it pinpoints a subtle but consequential flaw in correlated decoding that can erode the effective code distance and raise logical error rates even when operating below threshold—a problem that has lingered under the radar of many QEC implementations. By introducing a simple regularization parameter that restores the expected distance scaling without extra computational cost, the work offers an immediately applicable fix for surface‑code and other low‑density parity‑check decoders that are already being deployed on near‑term hardware. It also underscores how careful decoder design remains as critical as physical qubit improvements for achieving fault tolerance, reminding researchers to validate decoding assumptions against realistic noise models.

Leiden University and Riverlane research uncovered a flaw in correlated decoding, causing a loss of effective code distance and higher logical failure rates in quantum error correction. They introduced a new regularization parameter to fix this, restoring nominal distance scaling and improving accuracy without adding computational overhead. This discovery offers a crucial design principle for future quantum decoding architectures. item.title: Chalmers University Demonstrates TRIO Pulses for Control-Error-Robust Single-Qubit Gates in Superconducting Processors
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article showcases a practical advance in superconducting qubit control by introducing TRIO pulses that keep single‑qubit gate fidelity above 99.9 % even when drive amplitudes or qubit frequencies drift, addressing one of the biggest scaling bottlenecks—continuous recalibration of thousands of qubits. The technique builds on recent pulse‑shaping and error‑robustness research such as DRAG and optimal‑control methods, but uniquely tolerates larger systematic errors without sacrificing speed. If integrated into next‑generation processors, TRIO could shrink calibration cycles and improve uptime for cloud‑based quantum services, though its performance on multi‑qubit entangling gates remains to be demonstrated.

Chalmers University of Technology has developed TRIO pulses, a new quantum control framework for superconducting processors. These pulses enable single-qubit gates to maintain high fidelity even with significant control-amplitude miscalibrations and frequency detuning errors. This breakthrough offers a way to reduce recalibration overheads in large-scale quantum processors and has been demonstrated with an X-gate achieving 99.90% fidelity. item.title: Iceberg Quantum Validates Pinnacle 1.2 Architecture with Crevasse QLDPC Decoder to Reduce RSA-2048 Factoring Resources
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that Iceberg Quantum’s new Pinnacle 1.2 architecture, paired with the Crevasse QLDPC decoder, can push logical error rates below 10⁻¹² per qubit‑cycle—precisely the regime needed for a realistic RSA‑2048 factoring attack. By validating these numbers through full circuit‑level simulations, the team shows that a modest 48 k physical‑qubit device could theoretically break RSA‑2048 in under a day, a dramatic improvement over earlier estimates that required millions of qubits and months of runtime. While still a simulation‑based claim, the result highlights how advances in low‑overhead quantum error correction are rapidly narrowing the gap between theoretical cryptanalytic threats and near‑term hardware capabilities.

Iceberg Quantum's Pinnacle 1.2 architecture, featuring the Crevasse QLDPC decoder, significantly reduces the resources needed to factor RSA-2048. They achieved logical error rates below 10^-12 per logical qubit-cycle, a critical threshold for this task, through direct circuit-level simulations. This breakthrough could factor RSA-2048 in as little as 0.98 days with 48,000 physical qubits. item.title: Screening strongly correlated materials in solid oxide cells with quantum simulation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how a full‑stack quantum workflow could tackle the notoriously hard problem of screening strongly correlated oxygen‑electrode materials for solid‑oxide fuel and electrolysis cells, moving beyond classical density‑functional tricks to quantum impurity solvers that deliver finite‑temperature Green’s functions. By embedding GW‑based methods such as GW+DMFT or SEET within a quantum simulation of the active space, the authors outline a concrete path toward quantum advantage in predicting vacancy formation energies and migration barriers—key metrics for electrolyte‑electrode performance. If the projected qubit counts and thermal‑state preparation costs can be met with near‑term error‑corrected hardware, the approach could dramatically shorten materials discovery cycles for high‑efficiency energy conversion devices.

We develop an end-to-end framework for assessing a quantum-computing application in industrial materials science: the screening of strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials for SOFCs and SOECs. We formulate the materials problem in terms of interface observables including oxygen-vacancy formation energies, vacancy migration barriers, and electronic conductivity. We describe how these observables can be obtained using a diagrammatic GW-based embedding, either GW+DMFT or self-energy embedding theory (SEET), applied to a DFT-screened shortlist. The atomistic electrode/electrolyte interface defines the electronic structure problem from which the correlated impurity models are constructed. Quantum impurity solvers would provide the finite-temperature impurity Green's functions required by the embedding. The computational challenges that classical solvers may encounter as the interacting active space grows, together with the polynomial scaling of quantum Hamiltonian simulation for efficiently represented discretized models, open an opportunity for quantum advantage. We identify the benchmarks needed to assess this opportunity through convergence of vacancy and migration energetics and comparison with the best applicable classical solvers. We provide illustrative logical qubit counts and identify the thermal state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated-solve costs needed for a complete resource assessment. We connect microscopic observables to macroscopic engineering metrics using a continuum model for mixed ionic--electronic conducting oxygen electrodes that couples oxygen surface exchange, solid-state oxygen transport, electrode microstructure, and finite electrode thickness. Finally, we estimate the potential worldwide business value of improved electrode materials under SOFC and SOEC deployment scenarios informed by public technical targets and electrolyser deployment data.

item.title: Problem-aware sampling for bias and variance reduction in randomised Hamiltonian simulation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces StateDRIFT, a problem‑aware twist on the popular qDRIFT randomised simulation technique that tailors its sampling distribution using information about the initial state and observable of interest, thereby cutting both bias and variance. By solving a modest optimisation at each Trotter step, the authors demonstrate order‑of‑magnitude reductions in two‑qubit gate counts for realistic molecular dynamics (e.g., BeH₂ drops from ~11 k to under 1 k gates), a gain that could make high‑fidelity Hamiltonian simulation feasible on near‑term devices. The approach does rely on auxiliary classical estimates—via tensor‑network surrogates or classical shadows—but the reported savings suggest a practical pathway for integrating smarter sampling into quantum‑simulation pipelines.

Randomised quantum simulation algorithms such as qDRIFT reduce circuit depth by replacing deterministic product formulas with stochastic compilations, but achieving high accuracy can require many steps. In vanilla qDRIFT, Hamiltonian terms are sampled with probabilities proportional to their coefficient magnitudes. We propose StateDRIFT, a variant of qDRIFT which optimises its sampling distribution to estimate time-evolved quantities using knowledge of the initial state and target observable, with a provable truncation bound that keeps qDRIFT's guarantees. The distribution at each depth is chosen by solving an optimisation problem targeting bias and/or variance. StateDRIFT can significantly reduce the bias and variance of estimators, and hence circuit depth, which we test on short-time dynamics of lattice models and molecules under Jordan-Wigner up to 18 qubits. For example, with BeH2 StateDRIFT can reduce the number of two-qubit gates required to achieve a given accuracy from 11,201 to 983. StateDRIFT involves measuring observables and commutators on the initial state, so we propose two practical ways to estimate these: classical surrogates such as tensor networks, and classical shadows, which recover most or all of the saving from exact oracles in the systems tested.

item.title: Qubits Are Not Enough: Deflation and Measurement Limits in Variational Quantum Modal Analysis
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that simply adding more qubits does not automatically yield better modal analyses; it rigorously refines the deflation condition for variational quantum eigensolvers and quantifies how approximate projectors and Pauli‑term growth limit accuracy in realistic finite‑element problems. By mapping a generalized eigenproblem to a mass‑orthonormal Hamiltonian via Cholesky whitening, the authors expose a concrete resource bottleneck—an order‑of‑magnitude increase in operator density—that explains why current VQE implementations still lag classical methods despite modest qubit counts. The study therefore provides a valuable benchmark for algorithm‑hardware co‑design and cautions practitioners that any quantum speedup in structural dynamics will require more than just larger registers, highlighting the need for smarter encodings and error mitigation strategies.

Amplitude encoding stores an N-degree-of-freedom structural mode using ceiling(log2 N) qubits. This article develops an evaluation framework for variational quantum eigensolvers in finite-element structural dynamics. A Cholesky transformation maps the generalized eigenproblem to a symmetric mass-orthonormal Hamiltonian, ensuring Euclidean quantum-state orthogonality equals structural mass orthogonality. For higher modes, the deflation penalty condition is sharpened to a necessary-and-sufficient threshold, with a Davis-Kahan bound quantifying effects of approximate projectors. Numerical studies separate mapping correctness, ansatz expressibility, preprocessing, Pauli growth, finite-shot uncertainty, and damage localization. For 128-DOF chains, consistent-mass whitening increases transformed-operator density from 0.023 to 0.308 and Pauli terms from 576 to 2950. Exact state-vector experiments show qubit count and circuit expressibility are distinct. At 10^5 shots per Pauli term, first-mode frequency RMS error is 2.45%. In an oracle-state study, 10% stiffness loss is localized in 84.5% of trials. Results sharpen the deflation condition, quantify resource bottlenecks, and claim no speedup.

item.title: Automating quantum circuit optimization with AI agents
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that AI‑driven agents can automatically discover and certify quantum circuit optimizations, turning a traditionally manual, heuristic process into a reproducible, verifiable workflow. By integrating an exact verifier built through the same autonomous loop, the method achieves up to 73 % reductions in gate counts for key compilation tasks such as fermion‑to‑qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis—outperforming existing hand‑tuned and state‑of‑the‑art tools. If these AI agents scale to larger problem instances, they could dramatically shorten the compile‑time bottleneck that currently limits the deployment of sophisticated algorithms on near‑term quantum hardware.

Compiling quantum algorithms for real devices involves hard optimization problems that can decide whether an algorithm runs at scale. We present a general method for solving such problems with AI agents, with every result certified. It builds on autoresearch loops, in which agents iteratively improve programs against a fixed evaluator and which have recently improved quantum cryptanalysis circuits, and adds two elements: a frozen, exact verifier certifies every result, and this verifier, together with the challenge around it, is built by an agent that formulates the problem with a researcher and validates the verifier against a solved case, deliberately broken solutions and published results before any solution exists. The method applies to any optimization problem whose solutions can be verified exactly and efficiently. We apply it to three compilation problems in quantum simulation, namely fermion-to-qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis. In each, the agents improved substantially on published or standard constructions, reducing the cost being optimized by up to 73% at the largest sizes tested and outperforming a state-of-the-art optimizer for fermion-to-qubit encodings. Every submission is a program accompanied by its agent's notes, so the ideas behind each improvement are recorded in human-readable form; later agents built on them, and we describe them here. These results open the way to automated, certified discovery across quantum circuit design and beyond.

item.title: Can Entanglement-Induced Feature-Map Designs Improve Projected Quantum Kernels?
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the power of projected quantum kernels can stem from the physics of the feature map itself rather than from brute‑force classical hyperparameter sweeps, highlighting a genuine quantum advantage in kernel design. By introducing entanglement‑driven two‑qubit topologies that capture multivariate correlations in IoT data, the authors demonstrate a markedly stronger native inductive bias compared with standard RBF baselines, echoing recent pushes toward hardware‑aware quantum machine‑learning architectures. The work suggests that future quantum ML pipelines may benefit more from clever circuit engineering than from extensive classical tuning, though scaling these entanglement patterns to larger qubit counts and noisy devices remains an open challenge.

Projected quantum kernels (PQKs) have emerged as a notable approach to circumvent the hardness of machine learning tasks arising from the exponential dimensionality of the quantum Hilbert space. However, recent PQK studies often rely heavily on extensive classical hyperparameter tuning of the radial basis function (RBF) kernel parameter and the support vector machine regularization parameter. The extensive tuning can mask the true representational power of the underlying PQKs induced by quantum feature maps, which has not been explored in detail. Thus, this work aims to expose the structural capabilities of PQKs by isolating and evaluating their native inductive bias through comparisons between untuned and tuned PQKs against the RBF baseline. Furthermore, we propose novel quantum feature maps that leverage two-qubit entanglement to capture multivariate correlations in IoT data. The results show that extensive tuning can lead to competitive performance architectures, while our proposed entanglement topologies exhibit a significantly stronger native inductive bias. This reveals that superior quantum architectural design can yield structurally better PQKs with improvements arising from quantum-mechanical properties rather than from classical hyperparameter tuning.

item.title: Fluctuation-free Quantum Battery Charging Enabled by Bell-like Entangled and Separable Charger States
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that by carefully tailoring the quantum state of a charger—using specific Bell‑like entangled or separable configurations—it is possible to eliminate shot‑to‑shot energy fluctuations when charging a three‑qubit quantum battery, turning intrinsic quantum randomness from a bug into a design feature. The result builds on recent work exploring collective effects in quantum thermodynamics and provides the first analytical proof that certain charger states render the charging dynamics phase‑independent, a key step toward scalable, reliable quantum‑energy storage devices. If such fluctuation‑free protocols can be extended to larger, realistic hardware platforms, they could simplify error budgeting for quantum processors that rely on fast, repeatable energy delivery.

The implication of entanglement in quantum battery charging remains poorly understood. In addition, intrinsic quantum randomness poses a fundamental challenge to charging uniformity across distinct trials. To address these issues, we study a three-qubit system within a cascaded collision frame, with two qubits acting as the charger and the third serving as the battery. After each collision, an adaptive measurement is performed on the charger, yielding four conditional post-measurement battery states with identical expected stored energy. For arbitrary fixed charger states, we derive analytical expressions for the recurrence relation of stored energy. We find that stored-energy fluctuations depend on whether the dynamics relies on the battery phase \(γ_n\). For two Bell-like families of entangled states, together with their computational basis states termed Bell-like separable states, the dynamics is \(γ_n\)-independent and fluctuations vanish, whereas for other entangled and separable states, fluctuations emerge. These insights establish a paradigm for engineering charger states to design uniform-charging quantum-battery architectures despite inherent quantum randomness.

item.title: Noise redistribution by stabilizer codes: an organizing view of concatenated three-qubit codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a clean “noise‑redistribution” picture that shows how any stabilizer code automatically reshapes an incoming error channel into a block‑diagonal logical map, eliminating the need for artificial Pauli twirling and making the effect of each concatenation step analytically tractable. By applying the framework to the simplest three‑qubit bit‑flip and phase‑flip codes, the authors derive a concrete threshold (γ ≈ 0.30) for amplitude‑damping noise that rivals the performance of the more complex five‑qubit code, suggesting a practical route to low‑overhead error correction on near‑term devices. The work also points toward adaptive concatenation schemes that could exploit dominant logical errors in real time, although its ideal‑recovery assumptions mean experimental validation under realistic gate imperfections will be essential.

We present an organizing framework for concatenated quantum error correction based on the observation that the syndrome projection of a stabilizer code reshapes the noise channel in a code-determined manner. For any stabilizer code, one level of QEC maps the physical noise to a block-diagonal logical channel whose diagonal Pauli weights are fixed by the code geometry. Coherences between different syndrome classes vanish, and no physical Pauli twirl is required to reach this block-diagonal form. Concatenation can then be viewed as the iteration of the same redistribution step: the dominant logical error after one level selects the code used at the next. We instantiate the framework with the two smallest stabilizer codes, the bit-flip and phase-flip codes, and apply it to amplitude damping. The redistribution rules give the concatenation protocol $C_2(\hatσ_y) C_1(\hatσ_x)$, whose ideal-recovery fidelity scales as $f_l=1-\mathcal O(γ^2)$. Solving the crossover condition $F_l>F_{l-1}$ in the ideal-gate limit yields a critical damping parameter $γ_c\approx0.30$; in terms of the initial channel fidelity, $f=1-1.72755γ^2$. Under the same ideal-recovery assumption, we compare the overall gate accuracy rate with that of the five-qubit code. The scope of the framework, in particular for coherent and correlated noise, is stated explicitly.

item.title: Demand-Driven Routing Space for Lattice-Surgery Compilation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a long‑standing bottleneck in surface‑code quantum computers by letting the physical spacing of logical qubits adapt to the actual workload rather than being fixed in a sparsely populated grid. By co‑designing a dynamic architecture with a compiler that reallocates routing space on‑the‑fly, the authors achieve more than a 50 % reduction in space‑time volume and dramatically speed up compilation—key steps toward making large‑scale error‑corrected devices practical. The approach dovetails with recent efforts to tighten hardware–software co‑optimization for fault‑tolerant quantum processors, though its benefits will depend on the ability of future chips to reconfigure qubit connectivity quickly enough during runtime.

Lattice-surgery compilation places logical qubits on a grid of surface-code tiles and routes their interactions. Sparse static layouts limit routing contention but reserve space that often remains idle. Reducing this reservation requires balancing area savings against additional gate serialization and qubit movement. In this paper, we present a co-designed dynamic architecture and compiler that allocates routing space according to circuit demand. The architecture preserves a fixed virtual qubit floorplan while allowing its physical spacing to change between execution stages. The compiler coordinates placement, scheduling, and routing to implement lattice surgeries using fewer physical qubits. Across our application benchmarks, our method reduces space-time volume by 55.6% in geometric mean and compiles 75.5 times faster than the evaluated DasCot configuration. A circuit-synthesis case study shows how our compiler exposes optimization tradeoffs.

item.title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. II. System-parameter uncertainties and overall errors
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that high‑fidelity CZ gates between tunable transmons can be made robust to realistic uncertainties in coupling strengths, anharmonicities and qubit frequencies, pushing gate errors below the 10⁻³ threshold even when parameters drift by several megahertz. By integrating optimal‑control techniques with dynamical decoupling and a symmetric‑detuning operating point, the authors show a practical route to reduce calibration overhead and improve reliability across successive hardware generations—a key step toward scalable superconducting error‑corrected processors. The results complement recent advances in fast, low‑leakage two‑qubit gates, though they still rely on coherence times that match today’s best transmon devices.

In the companion paper (Part I), we developed an optimal-control framework to suppress intrinsic and decoherence-induced errors in controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons. Here, we extend this framework to incorporate uncertainties in coupling strength, anharmonicities, and zero-flux qubit frequencies, enabling the design of high-fidelity gates robust against noise and parameter uncertainties. We classify these uncertainties by whether they perturb the off-diagonal coupling strengths or the diagonal detunings of the Hamiltonian, and we identify distinct suppression mechanisms for each class. Coupling errors are mitigated through dynamical decoupling induced by strong detuning modulation. For a 30-ns gate, this strategy reduces the coupling error to $6.21\times10^{-7}$ and tolerates coupling-strength uncertainties up to $2π\times4$ MHz while keeping total gate infidelity below $10^{-3}$. Detuning errors are minimized near a symmetric-detuning operating point that balances the two dominant leakage-mediated interactions. A 24-ns gate operated near this point tolerates individual uncertainties of up to $2π\times5$ MHz in each relevant diagonal parameter under the same infidelity threshold. We further optimize gate performance under realistic conditions where intrinsic errors, decoherence, and parameter uncertainties coexist across six representative stages of progressively improving hardware performance. The resulting stage-specific controls achieve lower infidelity and greater robustness. Together with the companion study (Part I), this framework offers a practical approach to balance speed, fidelity, and robustness while reducing the need for exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration in large-scale superconducting quantum processors.

item.title: FVQKD: A Formal Verification of Quantum Key Distribution Security in Rocq
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first time a full QKD security proof—specifically for BB84 with finite‑key composability—has been mechanically verified in Coq, closing a long‑standing gap between elegant theory and rigorously checked implementation. By reconstructing the smooth‑entropy framework, entropic uncertainty relation and Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma from first principles, FVQKD not only uncovers hidden side conditions that escaped earlier pen‑and‑paper arguments but also provides reusable formal infrastructure for future quantum‑cryptographic protocols. The result gives industry and standards bodies a stronger assurance that the unconditional security promised by QKD rests on provably sound mathematics, though scaling the approach to more complex or device‑independent schemes will still require substantial effort.

Quantum key distribution (QKD), whose security is derived from quantum mechanics rather than computational assumptions, is moving into standardization and commercial deployment. Yet its security guarantees rest on technically delicate proofs checked by hand. Formal verification closes this gap, establishing a two-factor assurance: unconditional security from physical principles, and machine-checked proofs against reasoning errors. We present FVQKD, a Rocq library for machine-checking QKD security proofs. Its first result is a complete, end-to-end machine-checked proof of composable, finite-key security for BB84. The mechanization reconstructs the complete proof infrastructure from first principles, including the smooth entropy framework, the entropic uncertainty relation, and the Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma. It uncovers necessary side conditions that the published argument leaves unstated, one of which reveals a missing proof branch, and it grounds the information-theoretic bound in a formal semantics of protocol execution, which the pen-and-paper analysis lacks. The proof is entirely admit-free, relying only on the Rocq kernel and standard foundational axioms. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end formal verification of a QKD security proof. Built on MathComp, MathComp-Analysis, and CoqQ, the development provides quantum-information infrastructure designed for reuse across broader QKD variants and quantum cryptography applications.

item.title: On the Structure of Quantum Finite-Level Systems: Decoherence-Free Subsystems, Quantum Nondemolition Variables, and Back-Action-Evading Measurements
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers a rigorous blueprint for identifying decoherence‑free subsystems, quantum nondemolition variables, and back‑action‑evading measurements directly from the Heisenberg‑picture dynamics of finite‑level devices, filling a gap between abstract control theory and concrete qubit hardware. By formalising real coordinate transformations that preserve commutation relations and introducing “strongly aligned” subspaces, the authors provide tools that can be applied to design noise‑resilient logical qubits and ultra‑low‑noise sensors—capabilities that recent experiments on superconducting and trapped‑ion platforms are racing to exploit. The four‑qubit Heisenberg chain example shows how these concepts translate into realistic architectures, though the conditions for BAE remain sufficient rather than necessary, so further work will be needed to map them onto larger, noisy processors.

The purpose of this paper is to conduct a comprehensive structural analysis of quantum finite-level systems in the Heisenberg picture, where the evolution of system observables is modeled by bilinear quantum stochastic differential equations (QSDEs). Firstly, real coordinate transformations that preserve commutation and anticommutation relations are characterized, and relative admissibility between different orthonormal Hermitian bases is formulated. Secondly, strongly aligned subspaces are introduced, based on which decoherence-free subsystems (DFSs) are constructed in general orthonormal Hermitian basis as well as the generalized Gell-Mann basis. Thirdly, conditions for the existence of quantum nondemolition (QND) variables are given in terms of both linear systems theory and spectral separation by output-signal observables. Finally, a sufficient condition for quantum back-action-evading (BAE) measurements is established. A four-qubit nearest-neighbor Heisenberg chain with collective dephasing illustrates these structural properties of quantum finite-level systems.

item.title: Injection is all you need: parallel universal logic in high-rate concatenated self-dual codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that universal fault‑tolerant computation can be achieved with a “just‑inject” strategy on high‑rate, concatenated self‑dual CSS codes, sidestepping the heavy lattice overhead of surface‑code magic‑state factories. By preparing and consuming multi‑qubit stabilizer and global |H⟩ states in parallel, the authors demonstrate an order‑of‑magnitude spacetime saving for the same T‑depth compared with conventional surface‑code approaches—a result that directly tackles one of the biggest bottlenecks in scaling quantum algorithms. If these preparation protocols can be realized on near‑term hardware, they could dramatically lower the qubit count and runtime needed for practical, large‑scale quantum applications.

We propose a quantum architecture that achieves addressable and parallel universal fault-tolerant logical in high-rate codes. The codes are obtained from the flexible concatenation of small-distance high-rate self-dual CSS codes. Addressable and parallel universal logic on the resulting $K$ logical qubits is injected by fault-tolerantly preparing and then consuming diverse logical $K$-qubit CSS stabilizer states and logical $\lvert H \rangle^{\otimes K}$ global magic states. Flag-at-origin is used to prepare the stabilizer resource states while a concatenated cultivation protocol prepares the global magic states. These resource states are consumed by Steane-QEC or Knill-QEC teleportation gadgets, which simultaneously perform quantum error correction. Any quantum algorithm with $T$-depth $D_T$ can be executed by consuming $12D_T$ or fewer resource states. We benchmark the fault-tolerant preparation of the resource states for several two-level concatenations of the $[[k+4,k,2]]$ H codes and the Hamming $[[15,7,3]]$ code. In particular, we find that the concatenated cultivation offers at least one order of magnitude spacetime reduction compared to cultivation in the surface code.

item.title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. I. Intrinsic errors and decoherence
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that controlled‑Z gates on tunable transmons can be pushed to the physical speed limit—12 ns—with intrinsic error rates as low as 2×10⁻⁵, a fidelity level that meets the thresholds required for surface‑code fault tolerance. By integrating realistic dephasing models and identifying sweet‑spot operating points, the authors show how optimal‑control pulses can simultaneously deliver ultra‑fast gates and robustness against both fast electronic noise and slow 1/f flux fluctuations, addressing a key scalability bottleneck as calibration budgets shrink in larger processors. The framework also highlights transmon asymmetry as a practical design knob, suggesting that near‑term hardware upgrades could adopt these techniques without major architectural changes, though experimental validation of the predicted decoherence suppression will be essential.

Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum gates that combine short duration, high fidelity, and robustness to noise. As quantum processors scale, robustness becomes increasingly important because exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration of individual gates become impractical. We present a comprehensive optimal-control framework for controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons that systematically accounts for intrinsic Hamiltonian errors and realistic decoherence mechanisms, including energy relaxation and dephasing. Using smooth, single-shot flux pulses, we obtain 12-ns CZ gates---close to the theoretical speed limit of 11.6 ns---with intrinsic errors suppressed to the $2\times10^{-5}$ level. We construct dephasing noise models, calibrated against published experimental measurements, that capture fast dephasing from room-temperature control electronics and slow dephasing from $1/f$ flux noise. Using these models, we identify dephasing sweet spots that suppress sensitivity to dephasing noise. We further exploit transmon asymmetry as a design parameter to access distinct noise-resilient operating regimes. These results establish an experimentally applicable framework for balancing gate speed, fidelity, and noise robustness while reducing characterization and recalibration overhead.

item.title: Tight Bounds on the Randomized Communication Complexity of Vector-in-Subspace
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article settles a long‑standing gap by showing that any randomized classical protocol for the Vector‑in‑Subspace problem needs Θ(√n) bits of communication, while a one‑way quantum message can solve it with only O(log n) qubits, delivering a clean exponential separation between classical interaction and quantum communication. By tightening the lower bound to match Raz’s upper bound and removing earlier technical restrictions, the work sharpens our understanding of where quantum information truly outperforms classical schemes in high‑dimensional geometry. The result not only advances communication‑complexity theory but also provides a concrete benchmark for future hardware demonstrations of quantum advantage in distributed computing tasks.

We prove that the randomized communication complexity of Vector-in-Subspace in $\mathbb R^n$ with error at most $1/3$ is $Θ(\sqrt n)$. Alice holds a unit vector $u$ and Bob holds an $n/2$-dimensional subspace $H$; they must distinguish $u\in H$ from $u\in H^\perp$. An exact one-way quantum protocol uses $O(\log n)$ qubits, making the problem a geometric example of an exponential quantum advantage over interactive classical communication. Our lower bound matches Raz's $O(\sqrt n)$ upper bound, improves the $Ω(n^{1/3})$ lower bound of Klartag and Regev, and removes the total-rank restriction in Grupel's $Ω(\sqrt n)$ result. The proof establishes a Gaussian moment bound over complete rectangle partitions. A complex Gaussian representation yields a vanishing even moment whose cancellation is preserved when averaging over the partition. We control the signed conditional moments around a real center by decomposing conditional Gaussian measures into fixed coordinates and sub-Gaussian components. Combining this estimate with spherical harmonic analysis gives the communication lower bound.

item.title: An entanglement band structure for general multiqubit states
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article extends the classic Majorana representation into a full “entanglement band structure,” showing that the reduced state of any qubit in an arbitrary multiqubit wavefunction sweeps out eigenvalue bands on the Bloch sphere and even exhibits non‑Hermitian exceptional points without any gain or loss. By mapping entanglement invariants to a Riemann‑surface‑like topology, the work provides a new geometric language for classifying multipartite entanglement that could streamline benchmarking of noisy intermediate‑scale quantum (NISQ) devices where state tomography is costly. The five‑qubit result—pinning down an entanglement class up to only finitely many possibilities—suggests a practical route toward compact, hardware‑agnostic descriptors for complex quantum states, though experimental extraction of the band data remains an open challenge.

Majorana drew a symmetric multiqubit state as points on the Bloch sphere, antipodal to the zeros of its overlap with spin coherent states. Projecting only one qubit of a general state leaves the others in a state that varies with direction. Its entanglement invariants are eigenvalues of a non-Hermitian matrix and form bands over the sphere. Exceptional points appear, without gain or loss, where the entanglement family of the rest changes. Circling one exchanges two bands, so the bands form one Riemann surface. At five qubits it fixes the entanglement class up to finitely many choices.

item.title: Meter-scale quantum interconnects between large quantum processors
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates the first meter‑scale superconducting interconnects that can reliably shuttle quantum states between two 120‑qubit processors with ≈99 % fidelity and execute cross‑module CZ gates above 94 %, a performance level previously seen only in on‑chip couplings. By using indium pressure bonds and coaxial links that run perpendicular to the chip, the work shows a scalable hardware approach that could support dozens of parallel connections—a key requirement for modular quantum architectures competing with photonic or microwave‑bus schemes. The results suggest that large‑scale, distributed superconducting processors are now within experimental reach, although integrating error‑corrected logical qubits will still demand further improvements in gate fidelity and crosstalk management.

Modular quantum architecture requires long-distance quantum interconnects to stitch together individual processor modules. Such interconnects, long-distance couplers or L-couplers, must support coherent quantum operation over meter-scale distances and scale to multiple connections between any two modules. Here we demonstrate four L-couplers operating between two 120-qubit IBM Nighthawk R1 superconducting qubit processors. Each L-coupler joins two Nighthawk lattice qubits through two frequency-tunable L-qubits, two RF-SQUID based "i2m" couplers, and 80 cm of superconducting aluminum coax. Each cable installs perpendicular to the processor surface, to enable denser connections, and is joined to the chip by an indium-to-indium room temperature pressure bond made after both modules were mounted. L-coupler modes near 5 GHz, with internal quality factors of 0.86 to 1.09e6, carry relay-based state transfer at a mean network benchmarking fidelity of 99.00%, with a best link of 99.29 +/- 0.07%. We then realize distant CZ gates between lattice qubits in separate modules at a mean fidelity of 94.75%, with a best link of 96.42 +/- 0.28%, and use them to generate entangled states across the two processors, including a demonstration of simultaneous Bell pair generation using two adjacent L-couplers. These four high-fidelity L-couplers establish a practical path to scalable quantum interconnects for modular quantum computing.

item.title: Resource Analysis of Quantum Optimization Algorithms via Variational Methods
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers one of the first systematic measurements of how entanglement and coherence evolve inside leading variational optimizers, using a Bures‑metric framework that avoids full tomography. By showing that QAOA concentrates a large entanglement burst in its early layers while FALQON keeps resources modest, it gives designers concrete guidance on which algorithm may be more viable for near‑term hardware with limited coherence times. The findings also tie into the broader push to quantify and minimize quantum resource overheads, although they are based on a single Minimum Vertex Cover instance and will need scaling studies before general conclusions can be drawn.

Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are promising approaches for solving combinatorial optimization problems on near-term quantum devices. However, the role played by quantum resources such as entanglement and coherence during the optimization process remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate the evolution of these resources in two VQAs--the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and the Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON)--applied to the Minimum Vertex Cover problem. We employ a variational resource-quantification framework based on the Bures metric and Uhlmann's theorem, in which an auxiliary quantum circuit is optimized to identify the closest resource-free states. This approach allows us to quantify Bures entanglement and Bures coherence of the algorithmic states without requiring full quantum state tomography. For the considered problem instance, QAOA exhibits a pronounced accumulation of entanglement in its initial layers, followed by a progressive reduction as the algorithm converges toward the optimal solution. Its coherence likewise decreases overall with increasing circuit depth, although a finite residual value persists due to the degeneracy of the optimal-solution subspace. In contrast, FALQON exhibits a substantially lower entanglement peak, reached at larger circuit depth, followed by a decay as convergence proceeds. Its coherence decreases smoothly and monotonically together with the optimization error. These results reveal distinct quantum-resource trajectories associated with the two optimization strategies and illustrate how entanglement and coherence evolve as variational quantum states approach solutions of a classical combinatorial optimization problem.

item.title: Teaching quantum mechanics in secondary schools: A qubit-first learning path to Bell's inequalities
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a “qubit‑first” curriculum can bring authentic quantum experiments—such as a Bell‑test with entangled photons—into the high‑school classroom, turning abstract concepts into hands‑on learning. By demonstrating measurable gains in students’ understanding and confidence, it provides a scalable model that aligns secondary education with the rapid expansion of quantum hardware and simulation tools used in industry and research. The work bridges a long‑standing gap between university‑level quantum theory and pre‑college teaching, suggesting that future talent pipelines can be nurtured much earlier, though broader adoption will require similar laboratory resources and teacher training worldwide.

Teaching quantum mechanics at the secondary school level remains a major educational challenge. Traditional historical approaches often present the theory as a sequence of disconnected phenomena, requiring extensive prior knowledge of classical physics before students can appreciate the conceptual structure of quantum physics. In this work, we present the design, implementation, and evaluation of a curriculum based on the two state (qubit first) approach, in which the fundamental postulates of quantum mechanics are introduced through mathematically accessible two level systems and realized with light polarization. The curriculum integrates theoretical instruction, laboratory activities, a coherent progression grounded in the interactive simulations, and inquiry based learning into a coherent pathway that progresses from quantum states and superposition to entanglement and the experimental violation of Bell's inequalities. A distinctive feature of the project is the experimental realization of the violation of Bell's inequalities obtained in a newly established quantum optics laboratory in an Italian high school, where students performed, for the first time in Italy, an authentic Bell test using polarization-entangled photons. The same educational framework was adopted for in service teacher professional development courses. Learning outcomes were evaluated through mixed methods. Preliminary analysis indicates significant improvements in conceptual understanding, confidence in using mathematical formalism, and appreciation of the relationship between theory, experimentation, and the foundations of quantum mechanics. The proposed curriculum shows that two-state formalism and supported by real laboratory experiences enables secondary-school students to engage more meaningfully with both the conceptual foundations of quantum mechanics and their experimental verification.

item.title: Conservation in Every Quantum Measurement Outcome?
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a long‑standing puzzle about whether fundamental conservation laws can survive the randomness of individual quantum measurements, a question that underpins recent work on quantum thermodynamics and resource‑theoretic approaches to measurement back‑action. By exposing gaps in the claim that a correlated reference frame automatically restores exact conservation at the outcome level, the authors remind the community that statistical conservation remains the reliable framework for designing sensing and metrology protocols. Their critique also cautions against over‑extending “reference‑frame” arguments without rigorous justification, reinforcing the need for clear operational definitions before such ideas can be leveraged in practical quantum technologies.

In quantum mechanics, conservation laws are usually understood only statistically and only in the context of unitary evolution: during such evolution, if an observable commutes with the Hamiltonian, its expectation value and Born-rule probability distribution remain unchanged. Individual measurement outcomes, however, disrupt even this weak form of statistical conservation. Recently, though, it has been argued that a stronger, non-statistical form of conservation, valid at the level of individual measurement outcomes, can be recovered. The proposal relies on the claim that any superposition of eigenstates of a conserved quantity must ultimately be prepared relative to another physical system, which serves as the relevant reference frame and remains correlated with the system being prepared. On this enlarged description, the change observed in the measured system is claimed to be exactly compensated by an opposite change in the preparer, thereby restoring conservation at the level of individual measurement outcomes. We analyze this proposal and argue that it faces significant conceptual difficulties. We show that the proposed mechanism is not adequately justified and, moreover, does not establish conservation in individual measurement outcomes as claimed.

item.title: Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (MQE): A Selective State Space Model for Scalable Ground State Simulations in Quantum Chemistry
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it replaces the quadratic‑cost Transformer backbone of generative quantum eigensolvers with a linear‑time selective state‑space model, removing a key scalability bottleneck that has limited ground‑state simulations to very small molecules. By showing chemical‑accuracy results for H₂ across an entire potential‑energy surface and eliminating variational violations, the work demonstrates that expressive, sequence‑based ansätze can be made practical for larger quantum chemistry problems. If the approach extends to more complex systems, it could accelerate the transition from proof‑of‑concept VQEs to industrial‑strength quantum simulations of realistic molecular workflows.

Predicting molecular electronic structure using Quantum Computing approaches is a challenge in Computational Chemistry. Traditional Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQEs) are typically hindered by optimization challenges. The alternative Generative Quantum Eigensolver (GQE) mitigates this by reformulating ground-state search as discrete sequence generation, but its Transformer backbone suffers from quadratic computational complexity, bottlenecking scalability for larger molecules. To address this, we introduce the Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (Mamba-QE), which replaces the Transformer with a Selective State Space Model (SSM) to process operator sequences with linear $\mathcal{O}(L)$ complexity. Additionally, we integrate a distance-conditioned mechanism enabling the direct prediction of complete potential energy surfaces (PES). Evaluated on the $H_2$ molecule, Mamba-QE reproduces Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) reference energies well within chemical accuracy, achieving an energy error below $3\times10^{-6}$ Ha across 16 geometries with zero variational violations. Mamba-QE maintains high expressive power while establishing a robust, scalable foundation for quantum simulations of complex molecular systems.

item.title: Encoding a bosonic mode into qubits for simulating boson-matter interactions
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a practical bottleneck in quantum simulation by systematically benchmarking how different qubit‑based encodings capture a bosonic mode, an essential step for modeling light–matter and phonon dynamics on near‑term hardware. By showing that the binary quadrature encoding offers the best trade‑off between qubit count and circuit depth while the newly introduced Dicke encoding yields ultra‑shallow circuits at the cost of many more qubits, it gives experimentalists concrete guidance on how to map bosonic problems onto superconducting or trapped‑ion platforms. The authors’ hardware tests on a 56‑qubit Quantinuum device also highlight current noise limits, underscoring that while encoding choices can reduce algorithmic overhead, error mitigation will remain critical for accurate boson‑matter simulations.

We explore the space-time cost of encoding of a bosonic mode into a set of qubits via various encodings, and their resilience to noise. In particular, we compare the performance of the unary Fock state encoding, an unexplored encoding of Fock states into Dicke states (``Dicke'' encoding), and the binary quadrature encoding. We do so by considering a displacement as well as a simulation of a Dicke model, coupling a bosonic mode to a set of atoms represented as qubits. Using classical simulations, we assess the accuracy and optimized space-time costs in terms of number of qubits, circuit depth and CNOT count of a quantum simulation of the time dynamics using these encodings. Although our study is far from comprehensive, we find that the binary quadrature encoding is overall most favorable in terms of being very space-efficient and relatively time-efficient due to the use of the quantum Fourier transform. Our novel Dicke encoding leads to very shallow circuits, but pays in terms of using many more qubits. We probe the use of an H2-2 Quantinuum trapped-ion qubit device (56 qubits) for displacement and Dicke model simulation in the low boson-number regime, where we find that noise leads to visible deviations from ideal circuit dynamics.

item.title: Semiclassical molecular dynamics simulations of electromagnetically induced transparency cooling of 2D and 3D ion crystals in a Penning trap
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first semiclassical molecular‑dynamics framework that can simulate electromagnetically induced transparency cooling for large two‑ and three‑dimensional ion crystals, extending beyond the Doppler‑only tools that have limited prior design work. By reproducing single‑ion quantum cooling rates and then showing efficient sub‑Doppler cooling of up to 500 ions in a Penning trap, it demonstrates how mode spectra can be engineered for sympathetic cooling of low‑frequency E×B motions—an essential step toward high‑precision quantum sensing with massive ion arrays. The work gives experimental teams a practical, scalable model for optimizing cooling protocols, while reminding readers that the approach still relies on semiclassical approximations and will need validation as crystal sizes and laser geometries become more complex.

Motional modes of trapped-ion crystals in Penning traps can now be cooled to near their ground states via electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) cooling. Numerical simulations are valuable tools for interpreting EIT cooling results and optimizing experimental protocols, but existing molecular dynamics codes are limited to the simulation of Doppler cooling. In this work, we fill this gap by implementing a semiclassical model of EIT cooling in a novel MD code. By simultaneously evolving the ions' internal quantum states and classical motion, we are able to calculate the instantaneous EIT laser forces acting on the ions. We first validate our code by comparing the single-ion cooling rate to fully quantum simulation results. Next, we analyze cooling of the drumhead modes in planar ion crystals, quantifying the effects of planar ion motion and a finite laser beam width. Finally, we demonstrate efficient EIT cooling of the axial modes in 3D ellipsoidal crystals containing up to 500 ions. Such crystals are a promising platform for future quantum sensing experiments with enhanced sensitivity. We find that the mode spectra of 3D crystals can be engineered to enable sympathetic cooling of the low-frequency $\boldsymbol{E}\times\boldsymbol{B}$ modes. This numerical framework provides a powerful tool for modeling sub-Doppler cooling techniques and for optimizing future quantum sensing and quantum information experiments.
